newsitem.title: THAILAND: Outgoing Thai PM sees king, coalition deadlocked.
newsitem.headline: Outgoing Thai PM sees king, coalition deadlocked.

text.p: Outgoing Thai premier Banharn Silpa-archa met the king late on Tuesday but he made no comments on whether he had submitted his resignation to the palace.

The prime minister sought an audience with King Bhumibol Adulyadej as rumours swirled in Bangkok that Banharn might dissolve parliament after meeting the monarch or might back a former premier Chatichai Choonhavan as his successor.
Cabinet secretary Wissanu Krua-ngam, who accompanied Banharn, said: "There will be no announcement or anything by tonight or tomorrow morning."
Banharn, who was forced by key coalition partners on Saturday to declare his resignation within seven days, is in a standoff with them over picking a suitable successor from the six-party coalition.
Coalition allies had agreed to back him in a no-confidence vote in parliament on Saturday only if he agreed to quit.
Politicians and analysts had also speculated that if the impasse over the choice of a new leader was not resolved soon, Banharn might dissolve parliament and call snap elections.
Rumours flew around the Thai stock market late on Tuesday that Banharn may dissolve parliament or back former premier Chatichai Choonhavan as a compromise choice for his successor.
Chatichai heads the opposition Chart Pattana party and was premier during 1988-91, when Thailand's economy boomed, but he was ousted in a military coup in February 1991.
Politicians speculated that his party might join Banharn's coalition and Chatichai would be declared Banharn's successor.
Some broadcasters had analysts speculating Banharn would dissolve parliament later on Wednesday after meeting the king.
Signs of discord over his successor appeared on Tuesday as a top adviser and elder in Banharn's Chart Thai party, which leads the ruling coalition, declared his right to the top job.
Pramarn Adireksarn, whom Banharn supporters have pushed to succeed him, claimed he was in line for the top post because he was a senior Chart Thai leader and had party support.
His statement frustrated some coalition members who had openly been lobbying for Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who was behind efforts to oust Banharn, analysts said.
Banharn has declined to talk to reporters since his ouster over the weekend, and his supporters say he might nominate someone else as his successor to spite Chavalit.
Chavalit leads the New Aspiration Party (NAP), the second largest party in the coalition with 57 seats of the 209 seats the coalition controls. There are 391 seats in parliament.
Banharn could also hit back at detractors by calling a snap election instead of handing Chavalit the post, another source said.
Earlier, a spokesman for Banharn's Chart Thai party told reporters that the choice of Banharn's successor would come from within the six-party coalition.
A senior government source told Reuters that Banharn was unlikely to announce his successor before Friday, a day before he had pledged to quit the top post.
